Team Pistachio · RealPDE

Our RealPDE solution

Validation forecasts and solution details.

Roy Segal · October 2026

The Problem

RealPDE asks models to predict real fluid flows. Our solution forecasts 20 future velocity frames from 20 observed frames on a 32 × 64 grid, together with uncertainty bounds. We train a SimVPv2/gSTA model on the released real recordings, then refine its predictions with small learned postprocessing networks.

Track 1 (T1) uses the current input window; Track 2 (T2) can also use earlier observations from the recording. The strongest T1 setup combines last-frame conditioning, locally scaled residual prediction, flow-aware augmentation, and separate final paths for point forecasts and uncertainty. T2 keeps that architecture and adds seven causal history features summarizing observations before the current window. Its weights stay fixed during inference.

The story is in the choices: what information to expose, which transformations preserve the forecasting task, and where the objectives benefit from their own capacity. Each chapter below explains the intuition, the implementation and the evidence.

How we built it

Explore the improvements we kept and the experiments that shaped our choices.

01What the model needs to see+

Make motion, a reference state, and physical scale easy for the model to use.

Why we explored this. Early controlled runs improved when we supplied explicit changes and summaries of the observed flow. Later, an error analysis showed that windows with stronger fluctuations also had larger forecast errors and more missed uncertainty bounds. That observation motivated normalizing by local fluctuation scale, then feeding the removed statistics back into the model. The aim was to simplify the forecasting task while keeping the physical information needed to reconstruct the flow.

Motion Recent changesReference Last observed frameScale Local flow statistics

Make recent motion explicit

The early nnU-Net experiments added temporal differences, summaries of the current input window, and a global conditioning path. A later compact U-Net gained from five-frame sliding mean, mean absolute deviation (MAD), and standard deviation channels. These three sliding statistics remain in the final model: they expose the recent flow level and variability at each location. This is context within the observed window; T2 history adds information from earlier windows.

Last-frame conditioning and residual targets

We repeat the last observed u/v channels at every input step. Earlier frames describe motion; the last frame anchors its current position. This is already part of T1.

r = (y − xlast) / sŷ = xlast + s · r̂

y: future velocity · s: local fluctuation scale · r: residual. A zero residual predicts persistence.

Local normalization and statistical features

z = (x − μ) / s

Normalize each location by its recent mean and smoothed fluctuation scale. Feed those statistics back as channels, preserving the magnitude information.

Keep scale available inside the network

Supplying scale channels at the input was one step. In the earlier U-Net, we also used local means and scales to modulate features after each InstanceNorm layer, through SPADE. That improved every scored component and supported the hypothesis that normalization was suppressing useful magnitude information. SPADE was a successful U-Net experiment; the final SimVP model retains the input statistics and local-scale residual decoding.

Experimental evidence and implementation

Residual targets and normalization are established forecasting tools; GraphCast uses normalized residuals. We combine them with repeated last-frame channels and flow-specific local statistics.

The temporal-statistics change also improved the official Codabench final by 0.416149. In the subsequent validation diagnostic, observed fluctuation RMS and temporal-difference RMS had Spearman correlations of 0.962 and 0.966 with forecast-error RMS. Those associations motivated the local-scale experiment; they do not establish a causal effect by themselves.

These comparisons come from separate development stages. Scoring versions and some splits changed, so the gains are not additive. The repeated-last-frame concatenation comparison used different splits and has no isolated effect size. The early global conditioning and SPADE paths belong to the historical U-Nets.

The 18-channel stem combines u/v, last-frame u/v, sliding mean/MAD/standard deviation, window means, and log scales at 5×5, 3×3 and 9×9 neighborhoods. The plot uses a positive scale floor; training ties that floor to fitted channel statistics.

What did removing features teach us?

Deleting the larger summary stack did not help the early model. A minimal input replaced temporal differences, summary maps and global conditioning with raw fields plus time/x/y coordinates: best local quality fell from 82.9800 to 82.4384. At a matched training budget, the full feature stack still performed better.

Removing the coordinates from that minimal model helped slightly, 82.4384 → 82.5063, while remaining below the full model. This supports testing which information is useful; it does not establish that coordinate removal would improve the full feature stack. These are historical v6 ablations.

Evidence: experiment ledger, “Minimal-input ablations” (4 August 2026).

02View augmentations+

We introduced cropping to address the overfitting we observed.

The idea: vary the field of view so the model relies less on a fixed full-field layout and learns from local flow patterns.

Spatial cropping

Raw field: 64 × 128Native crop: 32 × 64

25% of the area, used in 50% of samples. Native crops expose fine local structures. Full-field stride-two views preserve global context.

Same split, seed, base recipe and 400 × 800 updates. The milder crops resize with bilinear interpolation; the retained crop preserves native samples. This tests the full crop recipe, not area alone.

Our quarter-area crop removes much more context than the 80–100% and 40–70% resized crops we tested, yet gave the best validation result. It keeps native samples and alternates with full-field views.

Related work

Small crops are established in vision: Torchvision's RandomResizedCrop defaults to 8–100% of image area. Spatial cropping also appears in PDE representation learning, including Mialon et al. (NeurIPS 2023) and PIANO.

Our experiment tests native quarter-field crops as regularization for supervised velocity forecasting. The result supports this particular recipe; those earlier works study different objectives.

Augmentation settings & evidence

Mixup is established; selecting partners from the same recording keeps the flow condition consistent. T1 development quality was 82.054000 for same-recording mixing versus 81.983664 across recordings.

T2 mixes every sample using a folded Beta(0.5, 0.5) draw. The crop studies used mixup probability 0.5 and alpha 0.2. Full-field views sample all four stride-two spatial phases.

Crops and reflections stay aligned across inputs, targets and history maps. Reflecting v intervals also swaps their negated lower and upper endpoints.

03Model architecture and training losses+

Share most of the model. Give point prediction and uncertainty their own final block.

Spatial encoder + seven shared gSTA blocks
↓
Point gSTA + decoderFuture velocity
SPS gSTA + decoderUncertainty features

A sharp forecast and a useful uncertainty estimate need different features. Splitting late gives each objective capacity while keeping most computation shared.

Residual and fluctuation-energy losses

Lpoint = Lresidual + 0.8 LTKE + 0.15 Lcoarse TKE

Selected T2 objective. TKE terms reward temporal fluctuation energy at two spatial scales.

Pixelwise error alone can favor smooth forecasts. Energy terms encourage the model to retain the flow's variation; quantile and SPS losses train the uncertainty bounds.

Architecture choices & experiment results

We build on SimVPv2/gSTA: spatial encoding, temporal translation and spatial decoding. Shared features with separate task heads follow a familiar multi-task learning pattern.

The first seven translator blocks are shared; the final gSTA block and decoder are separate. The point output is detached before the interval loss. Both objectives still train the shared backbone through their own paths.

Dedicated late SPS path82.151385

These milestones summarize complete configurations. T1 also used an MVPE loss; the selected T2 recipe omitted it. Interval training combines quantile-style supervision with a smooth direct-SPS objective.

Evidence: T1 METHOD §§2, 4, 8; T2 METHOD §§2, 4–5. Quantile-based uncertainty background.

04Learning uncertainty+

Learn bounds that adapt to the observed flow and reward useful precision.

Why we explored this. Our early calibration experiments showed that forecast errors carried structure: conditioning residual distributions on motion improved their bounds, and local spatial context helped further. The widest intervals covered more targets, yet did not earn the best SPS score. Those results supported two choices: let the input determine the uncertainty, and train for the score's balance between containing the target and keeping the interval narrow.

Observe the flow→Predict error bounds→Optimize interval quality

Let uncertainty depend on the flow

The first reference used one fixed residual interval per forecast horizon and velocity component. A small neighbor-aware convolutional model could instead use the local flow context to predict asymmetric bounds. We trained lower and upper residual quantiles, then calibrated them with conformalized quantile regression (CQR).

Interval = ŷ + [δlow(x), δhigh(x)]

ŷ: point forecast · x: observed flow context · δ: learned lower and upper point-error offsets.

Train for useful bounds

SPS rewards intervals that contain the target while penalizing excessive width, with a multiplier for forecast accuracy. We kept quantile training and added a smooth approximation of this objective. Smooth interval-membership functions supplied gradients; evaluation still used the hard scorer. With the original inputs held fixed, direct-SPS training improved over CQR alone. Adding input-window summaries and a longer fit improved it further.

Early calibration experiments and what they showed

In the first benchmark, the point forecaster was frozen. Calibration used trajectory-group folds; the following are held-out validation results under the early v6 scoring protocol.

Give uncertainty its own learned features

Later experiments trained the forecaster and interval head together, allowing uncertainty training to influence their shared representation. The final SimVP model carries this direction forward with a dedicated late SPS path, followed by learned interval refinement. The early standalone calibration heads were steps toward that design.

Joint-training result under the later scoring protocol

Under v9, a train-only CQR head on a frozen backbone scored validation SPS 42.7046 and local quality 78.4211. A joint model trained from random initialization reached 46.1662 SPS and 78.9916 quality. Calibration selected its epoch and validation remained untouched.

This compares training recipes, including their budgets and objectives. It supports the joint-training direction without isolating a single architectural change.

Evidence: T1 METHOD §8.4; experiment ledger, “Train-only SPS and end-to-end joint training” (9 August 2026).

05T2 history features+

T2 adds seven maps from earlier observations to our strongest T1 architecture. The weights stay fixed.

Past observationsAccumulate flow statistics
→
Predict this windowCondition on existing history
→
Update the stateAdd this input once

The past tells us what is typical. Comparing it with the current window reveals shifts in mean flow, variability and fluctuation energy.

2 mean differences2 log-scale differences1 confidence2 energy differences

Actual feature maps: Re 25,482 · AoA 15° · 180 prior frames. Each map has its own scale.

stem = stemT1 + Plinear(h) + Pnonlinear(h)

A small projection adds 3,537 parameters—about 0.018% of the T1 model.

Feature definitions and validation results

Mean and log-scale channels compare the historical flow with the current window. The energy channels use average variance within completed windows, separating fluctuations from changes in window means.

Confidence grows with prior-frame count. Running sums keep memory fixed; state resets at recording boundaries. Future targets never enter it. Mixup uses the common prefix before both windows.

Running statistics are standard. The seven-map representation and its injection into the spatial stem are our design choices: a 7→32 linear convolution plus a 7→16→32 nonlinear path, initialized as a zero correction.

06Prediction postprocessing+

Refine the forecast's energy and uncertainty with small learned correction networks.

Native + reflected views→Energy correction→Interval refinement

Averaging predictions can smooth fluctuations. Four small KE networks correct the forecast; a width CNN adjusts uncertainty bounds and shifts.

Postprocessing methods and validation results

Native and vertically reflected inputs run as a packed pair. Mapping back reverses rows and negates v; interval endpoints swap under negation. At fixed T1 checkpoint weights, this TTA step improved quality 82.105752 → 82.188882.

The full correction stage combines midpoint blending, analytic fluctuation-energy corrections, four small KE networks, a width CNN and fitted width calibration. These are lightweight correction models, not four full forecasters.

Fresh reproduction82.46703282.708458

The original archive transferred PP from an earlier T2 model. The final training package freezes the new forecaster and fits fresh corrections on 65 optimization recordings, keeping the 16 validation recordings separate.

The figure shows final bounds, not a before/after comparison. Evidence: T1 METHOD §§5–8; T2 METHOD §§4–8.

08What didn’t make the final model+

The experiments we moved on from helped shape the final solution.

We explored alternative features, architectures, and augmentations, retaining changes that improved validation performance. We stopped some trials early, usually when their initial validation results did not justify further training. Several ideas improved training metrics or individual scores without improving overall forecast quality. The results below reflect the configurations and training budgets we tested.

Features

More explicit flow geometry. We tested whether giving the uncertainty model a solid mask, distance to the boundary, and vorticity and strain features would improve its error bounds. With the forecaster, folds, seed, and training budget held fixed, validation SPS fell from 61.293 to 61.116. Enlarging the neighborhood reduced it further, to 60.783. Coverage rose, but the intervals widened and their score fell. These particular extra features did not improve the uncertainty model.

Removing the derived features. We tested whether a simpler input would reduce overfitting. Removing temporal differences, local summaries, and global conditioning together lowered quality. A raw-only variant recovered a little by dropping coordinates, but still trailed the full feature stack. Adding an explicit half-cosine time channel to that minimal model also hurt. We retained the derived features.

Feature ablation results

These are early U-Net experiments under the v6 scoring protocol. They concern features derived from the current input window, separate from the longer recording history available in Track 2.

Architectures

Trying other forecasters. The search extended beyond SimVP: we trained a ConvNeXt U-Net, SwinUNETR, a SimVP model with a parallel Fourier/FNO adapter, and several wavelet, recurrent, and temporal-attention variants. The completed 400-epoch ConvNeXt, Fourier-adapter, and SwinUNETR runs reached local quality scores of 82.0299, 81.7435, and 81.3539. We continued developing the SimVP recipe used in the final submission.

Learning a second correction with WDNO. We tried a wavelet diffusion neural operator as a residual refiner, including joint training and a version on top of a frozen SimVP. The frozen-base experiment produced only tiny changes. In a later fine-tuning run, the best quality equaled the base forecast with the correction gate set to zero: the refinement was effectively disabled. We dropped this extra stage.

CNO3D. We trained a CNO3D model with a dedicated uncertainty path and stopped early after 11 epochs. Its best validation quality was 72.2276, reached at epoch 10.

Comparing WDNO refinement with its own base forecast

We stopped the frozen-SimVP/WDNO run after 390 of 400 planned epochs. Its best refined quality was 81.8078, versus 81.8123 for the base forecast evaluated alongside it. The largest positive difference during training was only +0.0046. We stopped the subsequent fine-tuning run after 65 of 100 planned epochs. Its best quality was 81.8525, equal to the base with a zero correction gate; none of its validation evaluations improved on the corresponding base.

Architecture trial summary, including training budgets, best checkpoints, and refinement comparisons.

Augmentations

Gaussian input noise. Adding noise at 1% of each recording's velocity standard deviation produced a misleadingly low training loss. The noise inflated the local temporal scale used for normalization, reducing the normalized velocity-MSE term without a matching validation improvement. Best quality was 81.55, about 0.3–0.4 points below the comparable clean run. We removed this augmentation.

Mixing across recordings and resizing larger crops. Broadening mixup to different recordings gave a slightly lower score than using windows from the same recording. Larger crops resized to the model's input grid also underperformed the small crop kept at native resolution. We retained the same-recording mixing and native-crop recipes.

Perturbing temporal Fourier modes. An earlier experiment varied the amplitudes of low-frequency temporal modes to regularize fluctuation energy while preserving mean flow. It slightly improved peak TKE and reduced the training–validation TKE gap, but best overall quality fell from 82.0878 to 82.0392. Improving the targeted diagnostic was not enough to improve the forecast's combined score.
